targets.recommended_evidence_quality_note: [2026-08-02 failure-autopsy, V3-EXQ-869, confirmed failure_autopsy_V3-EXQ-869_2026-08-02, first-ever full retest, USER-CONFIRMED]: well-powered (30 seeds), pre-registered design cleanly separates manipulation-present (C0, iters=1, gaps 0.031-0.092 vs 0.015 floor, PASS) from production-persistence (C1, iters=3, gaps -0.004 to +0.004 vs 0.01 floor, FAIL; 0/30 seeds show the full predicted ordering). However the claim's own registration text and 2026-04-20 implementation_note explicitly name TWO mechanisms -- noise-scale modulation (built) and horizon-depth modulation (explicitly deferred to 'V4 reconsideration', matching the original 2026-04-27 lit-pull's actual recommendation and directly evidenced by Wikenheiser & Redish 2015). The wash-out-under-elite-refit pattern is mechanistically consistent with a noise-scale-only implementation being structurally insufficient against CEM's iterative refit toward a mode-independent value optimum -- not with the underlying claim being biologically wrong. Route: /implement-substrate to build horizon-depth modulation, then retest content persistence with both mechanisms active. pending_retest_after_substrate: true.

learning_extracted: A claim asserting multiple sub-mechanisms should be tracked as partially- vs fully-implemented; testing against only the implemented subset and reading a FAIL as pressure on the whole claim risks under-crediting the untested part.

CEM (and similar iterative-refit optimizers) can structurally wash out an initial-distribution-only manipulation if the downstream selection criterion is mode-independent -- a design principle worth generalizing.
The manipulation-check-vs-production-settings split (C0 vs C1) cleanly separates 'wiring exists' from 'effect survives realistic downstream processing' -- worth reusing elsewhere.
